page: Amazon Web Services r5d.metal is a bare-metal, memory-optimized server instance built on the x86_64 architecture. It provides dedicated physical hardware powered by Intel Xeon 8259CL processors running at 3.1 GHz, offering 48 physical cores and 96 vCPUs. The platform features 768.0 GB of DDR4 system memory clocked at 3 GHz, delivering an 8:1 memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. Storage is bundled via 3600 GB of high-speed local NVMe SSD instance storage, paired with a baseline network bandwidth of 25 Gbps. The server operates without dedicated GPUs and supports hardware virtualization extensions alongside instruction sets such as AVX-512 and AES.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong parallel compute and memory throughput. The server scores in the top tier for multi-core compute in stress-ng (82012.9) and the PassMark CPU suite (57042.31), bolstered by high instruction throughput in compilation (44143.0) and ray tracing tasks. Large-block uncached read memory bandwidth reaches 224.13 GB/sec, while cached read bandwidth delivers 4539.97 GB/sec. These characteristics translate to robust transactional operations, evidenced by 74.42 million Redis SET operations per second and 44.25 GB/sec in static web serving throughput.

Tradeoffs manifest primarily in single-threaded tasks and text-generation workloads. Single-core performance across Geekbench and stress-ng falls in the middle range, reflecting standard per-core frequencies of the Intel Xeon 8259CL generation. Furthermore, the absence of hardware accelerators results in weak to poor text generation throughput for large language models, generating only 4.99 tokens per second on a 7B parameter model. Cost efficiency is optimized for memory-dense, read-heavy workloads where massive RAM capacity and direct-attached NVMe storage remove the overhead of virtualization and external network block storage.

The Amazon Web Services r5d.metal is directly aligned with large-scale in-memory databases, distributed caching layers such as Redis or Memcached, high-throughput database operations, and big data ETL pipelines that require fast local scratch disks and dedicated bare-metal access.
